summary: Describes how SSH can use the GSS-API for authentication and key exchange. It defines a user authentication method that uses a chosen GSS-API mechanism, and key exchange methods that use GSS-API to authenticate a Diffie-Hellman exchange. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Lets a computer reuse a login you already did, such as with a company ticket, to prove who you are for a secure remote session.

questions: how does kerberos login work with ssh
what is the ssh null host key algorithm
subtitle: How SSH can reuse a GSS-API login, such as Kerberos, to authenticate the server and the user.

tldr.problem: SSH normally relies on host public keys and passwords or user keys, but sites that already run a GSS-API security system, such as Kerberos, want SSH to use that instead.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a family of key exchange methods that authenticate a Diffie-Hellman exchange with GSS-API, plus two user authentication methods, gssapi-with-mic and gssapi-keyex, and a null host key algorithm.
tldr.outcome: Any GSS-API mechanism can be used with SSH. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 8732 and RFC 9142.

today: RFC 4462 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8732 and RFC 9142, so read those alongside it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Reusing GSS-API Inside SSH
sections.content:
The Generic Security Service API (GSS-API) gives programs security services in a way that does not depend on the underlying mechanism. RFC 4462 describes how SSH can use it for both key exchange and user authentication, so that any GSS-API mechanism can be used with the Secure Shell protocol.

To do this it defines a family of key exchange methods, two user authentication methods and a new host key algorithm. The document is meant to be read after the SSH architecture, transport and user authentication documents, and it uses their terminology without explaining it.

One naming trap is called out: the service name in an SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST is an SSH service name, currently only ssh-connection, and has nothing to do with GSS-API service names.
sections.eli5: SSH is a secure tunnel between two computers. This document lets it borrow a login system you already use, instead of inventing a new one.

sections.title: GSS-API-Authenticated Key Exchange
sections.content:
The key exchange methods combine the Diffie-Hellman exchange from the SSH transport protocol with mutual authentication through GSS-API. Because they need no public key signature or encryption, they may be used with any host key algorithm, including the null algorithm.

The client picks a random x and computes e. It then calls GSS_Init_sec_context(), and it MUST request mutual authentication and per-message integrity. The server calls GSS_Accept_sec_context(), and the two sides keep trading tokens while the server's status is GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED. If the context finishes without mutual authentication or without integrity protection, the key exchange MUST fail.

Once the context is established, the server picks y, computes f and the shared secret K, and hashes the version strings, both KEXINIT payloads, the host key, e, f and K into the exchange hash H. It sends f together with a message integrity code (MIC) of H, which the client checks with GSS_VerifyMIC(). A failed check means the key exchange MUST fail. Neither side may send or accept e or f outside the range [1, p-1].

The server may send its host key in an optional SSH_MSG_KEXGSS_HOSTKEY message. Because that key is authenticated by the GSS-API exchange, clients SHOULD NOT issue strong warnings or abort when an already-known host presents a new key, as long as the exchange succeeds.
sections.eli5: The two computers agree on a secret number in public, and the login system vouches that nobody swapped it on the way. If the vouching is missing, they stop.

sections.title: Group Exchange and Method Names
sections.content:
A variant lets the client negotiate the Diffie-Hellman group. The client sends a minimum, preferred and maximum modulus size in bits, and the server answers with a safe prime p and generator g. Servers and clients SHOULD support modulus lengths from 1024 to 8192 bits, and those are the recommended values for min and max.

Method names are built from the mechanism. Each name is a prefix plus the Base64 encoding of the MD5 hash of the DER encoding of the GSS-API mechanism's Object Identifier (OID). The three prefixes are gss-group1-sha1-, gss-group14-sha1- and gss-gex-sha1-, all with SHA-1 as the hash. Every such method is implicitly registered, with the IESG as owner of the method names but not of the underlying mechanism. Names starting with gss- are reserved for conforming future methods.
sections.eli5: The method name is like a label made from the login system's name, so both sides know which one they are using.

sections.title: The gssapi-with-mic User Authentication
sections.content:
The gssapi-with-mic method runs over the SSH user authentication protocol. The client sends an SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST listing the mechanism OIDs it supports in order of preference. The server answers with SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_GSSAPI_RESPONSE naming the first one it supports, or fails the request with SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_FAILURE if it supports none.

The two sides then exchange SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_GSSAPI_TOKEN packets for as many rounds as the mechanism needs. The client MUST request integrity protection, MAY request delegation, and SHOULD leave mutual authentication, replay detection and sequence detection off, since this process authenticates only the client. A new SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST at any time destroys the context and restarts the exchange.

The user name may be empty if it can be deduced from the GSS-API result. If the named user does not exist, the server MUST NOT accept the request, but it MAY disconnect or send a bogus list of methods so that it does not reveal which accounts exist.

To finish, a client with integrity protection sends SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_GSSAPI_MIC, a MIC over the session identifier and request fields. This binds the context to the SSH session keys, so a man-in-the-middle cannot relay the authentication to the real server. Without integrity protection the client sends SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_GSSAPI_EXCHANGE_COMPLETE instead, and a server may refuse that by policy.
sections.eli5: You hand over a ticket from the login system, and then sign it with a stamp that is tied to this exact conversation, so nobody can reuse it somewhere else.

sections.title: Errors and Error Tokens
sections.content:
When a GSS-API error occurs, the server MAY first send a message with the major and minor status codes, a text message in UTF-8 and a language tag. During key exchange this is SSH_MSG_KEXGSS_ERROR, and during user authentication it is SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_GSSAPI_ERROR.

If a GSS-API call returns an error status along with a token, that error token SHOULD be sent to the peer, so the security exchange can complete. The error message MUST be sent before the error token, because a client that processes an error token will likely disconnect without reading further messages. During user authentication a server's error token is followed by SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_FAILURE, while a client's error token is followed by a new request or by disconnecting.
sections.eli5: If something goes wrong, each side can leave a short note about why before hanging up, so the problem is easier to fix.

sections.title: gssapi-keyex and the Null Host Key
sections.content:
The gssapi-keyex method authenticates the user with the GSS-API context already established during the initial key exchange. It is one message: the user name, the service, the method name and a MIC over the session identifier and request fields. It may only be used if that initial key exchange was GSS-API-based, and a context from rekeying MUST NOT be used. The client SHOULD NOT try it more than once per session.

The null host key algorithm has no key material and provides neither signature nor encryption. It fits sites that require every key exchange to be authenticated with, for example, Kerberos, so the server has no host key to advertise. Any implementation supporting a conforming key exchange MUST also support it, and servers MUST NOT advertise it unless it is the only algorithm advertised. A server using it cannot interoperate with clients that lack it.
sections.eli5: If you already proved who you are when the connection started, this lets you just point back to that proof. The null key is for a clubhouse that has no lock because the guard checks IDs instead.

sections.title: GSS-API Considerations and Security
sections.content:
The client names the server using the host-based service name form: host@ followed by the server's hostname. Implementations MUST NOT use the results of insecure DNS queries to build that name. If a client cannot determine the name securely, it SHOULD NOT use this mechanism. Channel bindings SHOULD NOT be specified.

SPNEGO MUST NOT be used as the underlying mechanism. SSH already negotiates methods itself, and SPNEGO could subvert the client's preferred order of methods or cause interoperability problems.

The key exchange depends on the GSS-API mechanism providing both mutual authentication and per-message integrity. If either is missing, the exchange is not secure and MUST fail. Detailed error messages help debugging but may leak information, so implementations are RECOMMENDED to let policy control whether to send them.
sections.eli5: Always look up who you are talking to in a safe way, because a fake phone book could send you to an impostor.

sections.title: Message Numbers and Registrations
sections.content:
Key exchange messages use numbers 30 to 34 (SSH_MSG_KEXGSS_INIT through SSH_MSG_KEXGSS_ERROR) and 40 and 41 for the group exchange. The gssapi-with-mic messages use 60, 61 and 63 to 66, and number 62 is unused.

IANA registrations cover the gss-group1-sha1- and gss-gex-sha1- method families, the reserved gss- space, the null host key algorithm and the gssapi-with-mic and gssapi-keyex user authentication methods. The names gssapi and external-keyx are reserved to avoid conflicts with implementations of an earlier version. No new registries are created.
sections.eli5: Each kind of message gets its own number, like numbered mail slots, so everyone knows which slot means what.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXGSS_HOSTKEY
messages.note: Optional; not sent with the null host key.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXGSS_CONTINUE
messages.note: Repeated while more tokens are needed.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXGSS_COMPLETE
messages.note: Carries f and the MIC of H.

items.label: SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_GSSAPI_EXCHANGE_COMPLETE
items.desc: Client finishes when no integrity protection is available.

items.label: SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_GSSAPI_MIC
items.desc: Client MIC binding the context to the session.
